title: Sectioning: cryostat vs vibratome
objective: Choose between cryostat and vibratome sectioning for a given experiment.

steps.title: Thin enough to see through
steps.body:
Light microscopy needs thin tissue. Two common ways to slice fixed tissue:

- **[[cryosection|Cryostat]]:** tissue frozen in OCT, cut cold (often 10–40 µm). Fast, great for fluorescence.
- **[[vibratome|Vibratome]]:** tissue in agarose, cut with a vibrating blade in buffer (often 40–300 µm). No freezing, thicker sections, better for whole circuits.

steps.prompt: Match each method to what it's best for.
pairs: Keeping a flat tissue intact, no sectioning
steps.explanation: Cryostat = thin and fast; vibratome = thick and gentle; whole-mount skips sectioning entirely.

steps.prompt: You want to trace long, branching DRG axons through the tissue. Which method fits best?
steps.explanation: Thicker vibratome sections keep more of an axon's length in one slice, so you can trace branching. Thin sections chop axons into fragments.

variants.setup: You need to follow branching axons through the depth of a tissue.
variants.prompt: Thin 10 µm cryosections or 100 µm vibratome sections?
variants.reveal: Thicker sections keep more of each axon intact, so you can trace its path instead of guessing across fragments.

steps.title: Whole-mount: don't section at all
steps.body: For a flat tissue like gut wall, you can stain the **[[whole-mount|whole mount]]** — the intact sheet, no sectioning — and image the full network of nerve endings in one piece. The lab uses this to map how **[[DRG]]** afferents tile the **[[colon]]** wall.

sources.note: Uses perfusion-fixed and whole-mount tissue to map colon DRG endings.

reviewNotes: Sectioning choices; whole-mount tied to colon mapping.
